source_read: Publisher HTML (jamanetwork.com, JAMA Network Open 8(5): e2510077, published 13 May 2025; open access), reached through https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.10077 in my own browser tab at the first attempt (no check page): Key Points, abstract, all sections, Tables 1-3 as text (screen-reader copies), the flow-diagram caption and footnotes, article information, funding, funder role, conflicts of interest and the reference list (read to ref. 52). The table footnotes are on neither the publisher page nor the table images (the Table 3 image, 2158 x 1950 pixels, holds the table body only), so the footnotes of Tables 1-3 were read as text in the PubMed Central copy of the same article (PMC12076174). Not read: the flow-diagram image, Supplement 1 (eMethods, eTables 1-5, eFigures 1-5), Supplement 2.

claims.note: All Vickers-Smith figures in the magnitude match Table 3 and the Results: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70-2.06; n = 677), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09-3.89; n = 710); composite score 0.86 higher (0.34-1.38; n = 684) on the 0-15 scale. The comparison is between people who reported using strips in the 30 days before baseline and people who did not, all recruited at strip-distributing sites, not between people given and not given kits, as the claim says. Two qualifiers: (1) per footnote g of Table 3 (PMC copy), the adjusted overdose model included, as daily covariates, the follow-up risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used, which come after the exposure and may lie on its pathway, and it did not include injecting or past overdose; so 1.20 is not a clean estimate of the difference strips make, while the crude 2.06 is confounded by risk. (2) The authors did not measure intent and so could not separate risk-enhancing from risk-reducing behaviour, and anonymity prevented knowing whether anyone lost to follow-up died of an overdose.

anchors.extracted: Nonfatal overdose, strip group against comparison group: unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09-3.89), n = 710, P = .03; adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70-2.06), n = 677, P = .52; adjusted mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01-0.03) in both groups; modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02).

anchors.locator: Table 3, composite-score rows; Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Composite Score, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Composite risk-reduction score (0-15): adjusted difference 0.86 (0.34-1.38), n = 684, P = .001; 7.37 (6.63-8.11) against 6.51 (5.83-7.19); unadjusted 0.89 (0.44-1.35), n = 719.

Behaviour models (d): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever received strip instructions, past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week, part of week. Nonfatal-overdose model (g): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of week, composite risk-reduction score and number of times strips were used. Injecting is in neither.

Harm-reduction clients not representative and already seeking risk mitigation; no data on prior harm-reduction engagement; site messaging varied; behavioural intent not measured, so risk-enhancing and risk-reducing behaviours could not be distinguished; four-week follow-up; self-report subject to social desirability and recall bias; anonymity prevented assessing loss to follow-up, including fatal overdoses.

The authors note critics' argument that strips enable fentanyl use and say their finding that people using strips also report several overdose-prevention behaviours counters it (an association, not a test of that argument).

claims.overstatement: The list of what the overdose estimate was adjusted for is partly wrong. Footnote g of Table 3 (not shown on the publisher page; read in the PMC copy) gives the adjusted nonfatal-overdose model as baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus, on each drug-use day, drug category, study week, part of week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting and earlier (past 30-day) overdose were not in that model (past overdose and strip instructions were in the behaviour models, footnote d; injecting was in none). Suggested: 'after allowing for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and the drugs used, and also for the risk-reduction behaviours and strip use reported during follow-up'. Because those two follow-up variables come after the exposure and may carry part of any effect, the adjusted 1.20 may be biased toward no difference; the claim's conclusion (insufficient evidence) is unaffected.
claims.note: Everything else checks: 732 analysed of 1156 enrolled, at 14 strip-distributing organizations in Kentucky (5), New York (3) and Ohio (6), May to December 2023; four weekly surveys over 28 days (at most 37); nonfatal overdose = losing consciousness with someone having to revive the person, self-reported weekly for each drug-use day; adjusted mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01-0.03) in both groups; RR 1.20 (0.70-2.06), n = 677, compatible with 30% fewer or about twice as many; unadjusted 2.06 (1.09-3.89), n = 710; the strip group more often injected (75.1% against 56.6%) and used fentanyl (78.2% against 59.2%); modification by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02), the ratio falling with age; anonymity prevented knowing whether fatal overdoses occurred, so deaths could not be counted. The authors describe theirs as among the first individual-level studies of strip use and nonfatal overdose, consistent with 'the only study read'. They had hypothesized a lower overdose risk among people using strips (Introduction, 4th paragraph); the crude estimate went the other way.

Among the first studies of individual-level strip use and nonfatal overdose; crude difference, none after adjustment, which the authors attribute to the strip group's concurrent risk-conferring (polysubstance) and risk-mitigating (testing strength) behaviours; strips alone may not be enough to reduce overdose risk.

claims.overstatement: Slight: the claim's population is people who were offered strips. Participants were recruited at sites that distribute strips, but the paper does not say each was offered them; 281 of 719 (39%) said they had never received strip instructions, 183 of about 308 (59%) in the comparison group (editors' calculation from Table 2). The sentence about this study itself is accurately worded.
claims.note: 414/732 = 56.6% (Wilson 52.9-60.1%, editors' calculation), as printed. Two qualifiers: non-response, 'don't know' and 'prefer not to answer' were coded as no use, so 414 is a floor; and 732 is the analysed sample, which required at least one drug-use day and at least two weekly surveys (424 of 1156 enrolled were not analysed; the share among all enrolled is not in the main text). The authors note that their share is far above the median of 19% in the literature they cite and may reflect recruitment at strip-distributing sites.

anchors.extracted: Over half the sample, 414 participants (56.6%), reported strip use in the 30 days before baseline; 318 did not.

Analysed sample of 732 of 1156 enrolled, restricted to people with drug use on at least 1 day and at least 2 weekly surveys during follow-up.

Strip use in this sample was higher than in other studies, where uptake is reportedly much lower (median 19%, ref. 14); this may reflect recruitment from strip-distributing sites, likely a factor in who uses strips.

claims.overstatement: 'Its overdose rate was twice as high before allowing for these differences and not clearly different after' implies that the adjustment removed the differences just listed (fentanyl use, injecting, strip instructions, baseline risk-reduction behaviours). Per footnote g (PMC copy), the overdose model adjusted for daily drug category (which partly captures fentanyl and opioid use) but not for injecting, strip instructions, past overdose or the baseline behaviour score; it did adjust for the risk-reduction score and strip use during follow-up. Suggested: 'twice as high before adjustment and not clearly different after allowing for demographics, drugs used and the behaviours and strip use reported during follow-up'. The behaviour models (footnote d) did not adjust for the baseline behaviour score or injecting either, which strengthens the claim's main point that simple comparisons mix any effect with who chooses to test.
claims.note: All figures match Table 2: fentanyl 312 (78.2%) against 177 (59.2%), n = 698; injection 311 (75.1%) against 180 (56.6%); ever received strip instructions 313 (76.2%) against 125 (40.6%), n = 719; each P < .001; past 30-day overdose 105 (26.0%) against 63 (20.5%), P = .10, n = 712. Heroin also differed (76.8% against 61.8%, P < .001), as did methamphetamine (64.5% against 56.4%, P = .03), opioid-stimulant combinations (65.7% against 48.4%, P < .001), state and race. 'Already reported more of the eight risk-reduction behaviours at the start' is stated in the text (values in eTable 4, not read). 'Ever having been shown how to use strips' paraphrases ever received strip instructions. The authors say recruitment at distributing sites is likely a factor in who uses strips, and that attendees are already seeking risk mitigation.

anchors.extracted: Strip group (n = 414) against comparison group (n = 318): fentanyl 78.2% against 59.2%; heroin 76.8% against 61.8%; methamphetamine 64.5% against 56.4% (P = .03); opioids with cocaine or methamphetamine 65.7% against 48.4%; injection 75.1% against 56.6%; ever received strip instructions 76.2% against 40.6% (each other P < .001); past 30-day overdose 26.0% against 20.5% (P = .10); Ohio 48.6% against 36.2%, White 85.8% against 75.4%.

The strip group used fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine and opioid-stimulant combinations more often and injected more; injecting was higher across drug categories and smoking more common in the comparison group; the strip group had a higher baseline composite score and number of risk-reduction behaviours (eTable 4); past 30-day overdose did not differ significantly.

Overdose model (g) adjusted for baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and daily drug category, study week, part of week, follow-up risk-reduction score and number of strip uses; not for injecting, strip instructions, past overdose or baseline behaviours. Behaviour models (d) included strip instructions and past overdose but not injecting or baseline behaviours.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed; the Table 1 footnotes, unreadable on the publisher page, are text in PMC12076174: always 2, sometimes 1, never 0 points, with throwing out drugs scored 1 or 0; testing the strength of drugs is defined as trying a small amount first to gauge its effects; using drugs slowly as spacing use out over time.

The Methods text lists these covariates, but the models differ (Table 3 footnotes, PMC12076174): behaviour models (d) adjusted for baseline state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week and part of week; the nonfatal-overdose model (g) for baseline state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injection entered no model; daily strip use entered only the overdose model. GEE: normal, identity link, compound symmetry for the composite (b); Poisson, log link, compound symmetry (e) or first-order autoregressive (f) for the count and the individual behaviours and overdose.
Locator as printed: Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph.

reporting_issues.note: Five behaviour aRRs above 1 exclude 1, with lower limits 1.04, 1.24, 1.10, 1.12 and 1.04; four lie between 1.04 and 1.12, as stated.

Answered by footnotes d and g (PMC copy): the number of times strips were used during follow-up entered only the nonfatal-overdose model, together with the follow-up composite risk-reduction score; neither entered the behaviour models. So the over-adjustment concern does not apply to the behaviour estimates but does apply to the adjusted overdose RR of 1.20 (adjustment for post-exposure variables that may carry any effect, which could bias it toward no difference); that model also omitted injecting and past overdose.

risk_of_bias.note: Serious overall and by domain, with two notes to correct. Confounding: the note says adjustment included injection, past overdose and strip instructions; per the footnotes injection entered no model, and past overdose and strip instructions only the behaviour models; the baseline behaviour score was not adjusted (confirmed by footnote d). For nonfatal overdose the model adjusted for post-baseline variables (follow-up risk-reduction score, strip-use count), which ROBINS-I treats as at least serious, so the fall from 2.06 to 1.20 may reflect over-adjustment as well as confounding by risk. Outcome measurement: Table 1 footnote b defines testing the strength of drugs as trying a small amount first, not strip testing, so the feared overlap does not arise; serious remains justified by self-report and the unvalidated score.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it moderate, one step above minor. The Key Points say the findings are 'demonstrating the role of FTS as a harm reduction strategy', and the Discussion says the association remained after adjustment for confounders, yet the behaviour models did not adjust for the baseline level of the same behaviours (higher in the strip group) or for injecting (footnote d), so the adjusted 0.86 may largely restate a pre-existing difference; the Discussion also reads this co-occurrence as countering the argument that strips enable fentanyl use. The abstract's conclusion is careful. For the senior author.

missed: The Table 3 footnotes (model covariates and GEE specifications) are not on the publisher page or in the table images but are text in PMC12076174; see key finding 7 and reporting issue 2. The card's analysis.covariates and outcomes.validity_norms fields can be updated from them, and the overdose model's inclusion of follow-up behaviours and strip use should be stated wherever the adjusted RR 1.20 is cited.

Introduction, 4th paragraph: the authors hypothesized a lower overdose risk among people using strips; the crude RR (2.06) went the other way and the adjusted one is null. The card does not record the stated hypothesis.

Table 2 footnote a (PMC): the 'Total respondents' counts exclude missing, don't know and prefer not to answer, whereas for the exposure those responses were coded as no strip use, so the comparison group includes people with unknown strip use.

The Discussion's explanation for the attenuation of the overdose estimate (the strip group's concurrent risk-mitigating behaviours) partly describes the model itself, which adjusted for the follow-up risk-reduction score (footnote g).
